title: Biologically repair the injured visual pathway

concept.text: Conceptual synthesis: This innovation would restore useful vision by biologically repairing the pathway that carries visual information from the eye into the brain. For severe optic-nerve injury, that means preserving or replacing retinal ganglion cells—the retinal neurons whose axons form the optic nerve—and restoring connections that allow visual signals to reach and be used by appropriate brain circuits. Regrowth alone would not complete the innovation: the repaired pathway would need to support useful seeing.

Conceptual synthesis: Repairing destroyed visual cortex is a related but distinct version of the challenge. Reconnecting an injured optic nerve could work only if the downstream circuitry were sufficiently viable or could also be repaired. Substantial cortical destruction would require reconstruction of functional brain circuitry as well as delivery of signals to it. Success in either setting would therefore establish a specific repair capability, without automatically establishing the other.

significance.text: Conditional significance assessment: Durable recovery of useful vision after severe visual-pathway injury would be a major advance because it would restore a sensory capability through biological reconnection. Its direct consequence would be that some people with an injured pathway could again use visual information. The extent of independence or improvement in daily activities would depend on the quality of restored vision, the injury, surviving circuitry and rehabilitation; those benefits would need to be measured.

Conditional significance assessment: Biological repair could potentially help some people for whom a visual-cortex prosthesis is unsuitable, but this depends on the reason for that unsuitability. Optic-nerve repair would not overcome extensive loss of the cortex needed to interpret its signals. Conversely, reconstructing damaged visual cortex would require additional capabilities beyond axon regeneration. The supplied material does not establish comparative eligibility, superiority over prostheses or restoration of normal vision.

Conditional downstream synthesis: A reproducible way to restore functional connections in the visual pathway could inform other forms of central nervous system repair. However, shared challenges such as neuronal survival, axon growth and circuit integration do not make repair interchangeable across organs or injury types. A visual-pathway result would provide a specific demonstration whose broader applicability would require separate evidence.

missing_breakthrough.text: Scientific synthesis of the proposed challenge: The missing capability is reliable biological reconstruction of an injured visual pathway that restores useful vision. Retinal ganglion cells must survive or be replaced; their long central nervous system axons must regrow, reach appropriate targets and establish effective connections. Each step is necessary to the proposed repair, but none alone demonstrates that visual information has been restored in a form the brain can use.

Engineering synthesis: A successful intervention would need to coordinate cell preservation or replacement with directed growth and functional integration across the injury. It would also need to establish that improvement results from repaired connections rather than spared pathways or other explanations. The supplied scientific artifact does not provide usable evidence about how the named experimental treatment addresses these barriers, its reliability or the limits of its effects.

Scientific synthesis of the cortical challenge: When visual cortex has been substantially destroyed, restoring an incoming signal is insufficient. Functional downstream circuitry would have to survive or be reconstructed so that the signal supports visual processing and behavior. Replacing tissue, establishing connections and recovering useful processing are distinct requirements; evidence for optic-nerve regeneration would not resolve them.

current_state.text: The supplied bibliographic information identifies a report dated 27 February 2023 titled “Regeneration and functional recovery of the completely transected optic nerve in adult rats by CNTF-chitosan,” with DOI 10.1038/s41392-022-01289-0. The research summary attributes optic-nerve regeneration and visual-system functional recovery after complete transection in adult rats to this report. This preserves the attributed historical finding, but the experimental results cannot be independently verified from the scientific text available in the supplied review.

The supplied review found that the retained PubMed copy contained only a cookie-access challenge, rather than an abstract or article text. Consequently, the supplied copy does not establish the article’s identity through its contents or permit assessment of lesion completeness, treatment methods, functional measurements, controls, durability, safety or experimental limitations. The earlier statement that the account rested on an inspected indexed abstract is therefore not substantiated by the retained evidence. This access limitation does not show that the reported result is false.

Evidence-scope assessment: The supplied material does not establish translation to severe human optic-nerve injury or successful reconstruction of destroyed human visual cortex. It also contains no usable bounded freshness-search record, so it cannot establish the state of either capability as of 1 November 2026. The retained source was retrieved on 11 November 2026; that retrieval date does not establish what had been demonstrated by the earlier cutoff. These are limits of the supplied evidence, rather than a field-wide finding that no further advances exist.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: Controlled human studies should show durable, objectively measured useful vision after severe optic-nerve injury, with converging evidence that biological reconnection mediates the improvement. Assessment should distinguish the effects of repaired connections from those of spared tissue or other explanations. These are proposed criteria for evaluating the innovation, not established consensus standards.
completion_criteria.label: Controlled human studies demonstrate durable useful vision through biological reconnection

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: Visual measurements should be accompanied by reliable improvement in real-world tasks. Reports should define the injuries treated, remaining retinal and brain circuitry, treatment timing, rehabilitation and follow-up duration, so that readers can understand who benefited and under what conditions. Long-term safety and independent reproducibility would be central to a convincing practical demonstration. The supplied evidence does not justify a particular numerical threshold for visual performance, duration or success rate.
completion_criteria.label: Visual improvements translate into reliable real-world task benefits

completion_criteria.text: Proposed separate demonstration: Repair after substantial visual-cortex destruction should independently establish reconstruction of functional circuitry, durable useful vision and real-world benefit. Optic-nerve repair alone would not satisfy that criterion. Reproducible results across defined injury types and severities would establish demonstrated breadth within those boundaries; finite studies would not establish universal repair of all visual-pathway injuries.
completion_criteria.label: Reconstructed circuitry restores durable useful vision after substantial visual-cortex destruction

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: NRL-08, “A visual-cortex prosthesis that restores useful, detailed sight,” shares the goal of useful vision but centers on a prosthetic route to visual-cortex function. NRL-16 centers on biological repair. Their relevance to an individual would depend on which structures remain functional and what each intervention requires. Neither concept’s success would establish the other’s performance or patient eligibility.

Roster-based synthesis: NRL-05, “Regenerate a severely injured spinal cord with functional reconnection,” overlaps in the challenge of restoring useful connections after central nervous system injury. NRL-06, “Replace lost brain tissue while preserving learned function,” is especially relevant to the cortical-reconstruction part of NRL-16. The distinctions remain consequential: reconnecting the visual pathway, restoring spinal-cord function and preserving learned function through brain-tissue replacement require different demonstrations.

Roster-based synthesis: NRL-02, “A general predictive theory of neural circuit computation,” could inform how reconstructed circuits are assessed or designed, while NRL-10, “Safe, programmable delivery to selected cells throughout the human brain,” could provide enabling delivery capabilities for some repair strategies. Neither a general theory nor brain-wide delivery is established here as a prerequisite for a successful, more localized visual-pathway treatment.

Roster-based synthesis: NRL-13, “Protect brain tissue during acute ischemic stroke,” overlaps where preserving injured visual brain tissue could retain circuitry needed for recovery, but preservation and reconstruction of destroyed tissue are separate achievements. NRL-17, “A durable bidirectional neural interface for movement and sensation,” overlaps in restoring useful communication with neural circuits, while retaining a different primary capability and demonstration from biological repair of vision.

unresolved_issues: Usable article text is needed to verify the 2023 report’s experimental findings, complete-transection model, treatment details, controls, functional outcomes, durability and limitations.
The extent of independent replication and any relevant human translation cannot be determined from the supplied material.
The state of optic-nerve repair and visual-cortex reconstruction as of 1 November 2026 remains unresolved because no usable bounded freshness-search record was supplied.
Which reasons for cortical-prosthesis unsuitability could be addressed by biological repair remains an open applicability question.
Appropriate quantitative thresholds for useful vision, follow-up duration and acceptable safety have not been established by the supplied evidence.

brief.title: Restoring sight by repairing the eye-to-brain pathway
possible: People who lose sight after a severe injury could regain useful vision through biological repair. This would mean reconnecting the optic nerve, which carries signals from the eye to the brain, so the brain can use those signals again.
For people whose injury destroys the visual cortex, the brain tissue that processes sight, recovery would also require rebuilding working brain circuits.
why: Restoring useful sight could help people use visual information in daily life again. Better vision could support greater independence, with benefits measured through the activities people can actually do.
Learning to rebuild working connections between the eye and brain could also inform efforts to repair other injuries to the nervous system.

sources.showed: The team reported regrowth across a severed optic nerve and recovery of visual function in adult rats. Axons, the signal-carrying fibres of nerve cells, grew across the injury.
sources.quote: The regenerated RGC axons not only passed across the lesion site but also grew into the distal degenerate optic nerve.
sources.cited_for: Biological treatment can support nerve regrowth across a complete cut in an animal model.
sources.not_established: This does not establish durable useful vision after severe optic-nerve injury in people.

sources.showed: This preprint reported nerve regrowth and restored vision after optic-nerve crush injury in adult mice. It suppressed DNMT3a, a protein that limits regrowth, in retinal ganglion cells (RGCs), the eye's nerve cells.
sources.quote: Selective suppression of DNMT3a in retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) by gene targeting or delivery of shRNA leads to robust, full-length regeneration of RGC axons through the optic nerve and restoration of vision in adult mice after nerve crush injury.
sources.cited_for: Suppressing a barrier within eye nerve cells can support regrowth and visual recovery in mice.
sources.not_established: The preprint does not establish safe, lasting recovery in people or repair after complete nerve severing.

sources.showed: Increasing nerve-cell activity alongside growth signals helped injured fibres reconnect with appropriate brain targets in adult mice. Some visual behaviours partly recovered.
sources.quote: Moreover, these regenerated connections were successful in partially rescuing a subset of visual behaviors.
sources.cited_for: Regrowing fibres can reach appropriate targets and restore some visual behaviour.
sources.not_established: Partial recovery in mice does not establish durable useful sight in people.

sources.showed: A combination of treatments prompted injured nerve fibres to grow back into visual brain centres in adult mice. Depth perception and other simple visual behaviours partly recovered.
sources.quote: We show here that with adequate stimulation, retinal ganglion cells are able to regenerate axons the full length of the visual pathway and on into the lateral geniculate nucleus, superior colliculus, and other visual centers.
sources.cited_for: Long-distance nerve regrowth can accompany partial recovery of simple visual behaviours.
sources.not_established: Simple animal behaviours do not establish reliable benefits in people's daily activities.

sources.showed: After injury from interrupted blood supply in mice, the team reported that cells reprogrammed into nerve cells joined local visual brain circuits and responded to visual stimulation.
sources.quote: Furthermore, following visual experience, the reprogrammed neurons demonstrated maturation of orientation selectivity and functional connectivity.
sources.cited_for: Reprogrammed nerve cells can develop visual responses and working connections within injured mouse brain circuits.
sources.not_established: This does not establish lasting useful sight after substantial destruction of the human visual cortex.

shown: Xiao Liu and colleagues reported nerve regrowth and visual-system recovery after complete optic-nerve severing in adult rats. Mouse studies by Silmara de Lima's and Jung-Hwan A Lim's teams linked regrowth into the brain with partial recovery of visual behaviours.
Yu Tang and colleagues reported that reprogrammed nerve cells joined injured visual brain circuits in mice and responded to visual stimulation.
missing: Controlled human studies would need to establish lasting useful sight caused by repaired connections rather than surviving pathways.
Recovery would need to produce reliable daily-task benefits, with long-term safety and independent reproduction.
Repair after substantial visual-cortex destruction would need to rebuild working circuits and restore useful sight.

milestones.label: Lasting useful sight through biological reconnection in people
milestones.explanation: Controlled human studies would have to show lasting, objectively measured useful sight after severe optic-nerve injury, caused by biological reconnection. This would establish that repaired connections carry usable vision.

milestones.label: Reliable benefits in everyday tasks
milestones.explanation: Visual gains would have to improve everyday tasks reliably in defined patient groups, with lasting safety and independently reproduced results. This would establish practical benefit and clarify who benefits.

milestones.label: Lasting useful sight after substantial visual brain damage
milestones.explanation: Studies would have to show rebuilt working circuits, lasting useful sight and everyday benefits after substantial visual-cortex destruction. This would establish a repair capability beyond reconnecting the optic nerve.

uncertain: The amount of restored vision, follow-up duration and safety needed to count as success remain open.
It remains unclear which injuries and amounts of surviving brain circuitry would allow biological repair to restore useful sight.
Whether these repair approaches can achieve independently reproducible recovery in people remains unresolved.

page.title: Vision restoration through optic nerve regeneration
page.definition: A treatment regenerates retinal ganglion-cell axons—the nerve fibres carrying retinal signals into the brain—and reconnects them with surviving visual circuits. These connections restore pattern vision, the ability to distinguish spatial forms, after optic-nerve damage.

goal.need: WHO’s fact sheet of 10 February 2026 attributes distance vision impairment or blindness to glaucoma in 7.7 million people worldwide. Glaucoma, ischemia and trauma can damage retinal ganglion cells and their axons. The NEI identifies failure of these axons to reconnect with their brain targets as the reason vision loss from this damage is irreversible.

statements.body: National Eye Institute, Audacious Goals Initiative
statements.quote: replace or regenerate cells in patients in order to restore useful vision, i.e. pattern vision, not simply visual reflexes
statements.context: The funding announcement identifies severe retinal ganglion-cell damage and photoreceptor degeneration as its two target conditions.

statements.body: Advanced Research Projects Agency for Health, THEA programme
statements.quote: THEA intends to test and evaluate the best therapies to repair damaged nerves
statements.context: THEA pursues whole-eye transplantation, including regeneration of the connection between the eye and brain.

completion.title: FDA authorises a treatment that restores pattern vision through optic-nerve regeneration.
completion.criterion: FDA grants marketing authorisation for a treatment whose approved use restores lost pattern vision in a specified optic neuropathy through optic-nerve regeneration. The supporting evidence establishes the regenerated pathway and its visual benefit. The applicable new-drug or biologics application satisfies FDA requirements for safety, effectiveness and manufacturing quality. The clinical effect follows the NEI’s stated regenerative goal; the authorisation supplies the external decision.
completion.set_by: FDA, marketing-authorisation requirements under 21 CFR 314.105 and the biologics licensing framework; clinical effect specified by NEI RFA-EY-14-001.
completion.threshold_quote: FDA will approve an NDA after it determines that the drug meets the statutory standards for safety and effectiveness, manufacturing and controls, and labeling
completion.basis: NEI explicitly requires human pattern vision after severe retinal ganglion-cell damage. FDA marketing authorisation supplies a published treatment-level decision covering clinical benefit, safety and manufacture. The regeneration mechanism and restoration indication delimit the capability being tracked; FDA’s general approval rule does not itself prescribe an optic-nerve-specific acuity gain.

milestones.title: Retinal ganglion-cell axons regenerate across an optic-nerve injury in an adult mammal.
milestones.criterion: Axons from surviving retinal ganglion cells grow beyond the injured region, establishing anatomical regeneration. NEI distinguishes this proximal growth from subsequent growth toward brain targets. In the study published on 21 May 2012, de Lima and colleagues reported full-length optic-nerve regeneration 10–12 weeks after crush injury in adult mice; the principal treatment and control groups contained 35 and 19 mice.
milestones.set_by: NEI Audacious Goals Initiative optic-nerve workshop, April 2015 report, section on axon growth; qualitative anatomical criterion.

milestones.title: Regenerated optic axons reach brain visual targets and support recovered visual behavior in adult mammals.
milestones.criterion: Regenerated axons reach central visual targets and anatomical recovery is accompanied by functional recovery in animal assays. In the mouse optic-nerve-crush study published on 11 July 2016, Lim and colleagues reported dorsal lateral geniculate reinnervation in 6 of 10 mice receiving combined treatment. Treated injured mice tracked approximately 23% of optokinetic stimulus trials, with 3 animals tested, versus 0% in 5 untreated injured animals. This establishes partial behavioral recovery in a traumatic-injury model.
milestones.set_by: NEI Audacious Goals Initiative optic-nerve workshop, April 2015 report, sections on target selection, circuit integration and functional assays; qualitative proof-of-principle criterion.
milestones.threshold_quote: Robust functional assays are needed for proof of principle in animal models to facilitate translation to human testing.

milestones.title: A candidate optic-nerve regenerative treatment is administered to a person under an effective IND.
milestones.criterion: A person receives the candidate after its investigational new drug application takes effect and applicable human-research requirements are met. An IND normally takes effect 30 days after FDA receipt unless the investigation is placed on clinical hold, or earlier following FDA notification. Life Biosciences announced ER-100 IND clearance on 28 January 2026 and the first participant’s dosing on 9 June 2026. These company announcements are not peer reviewed and do not establish human axon regeneration.
milestones.set_by: FDA, 21 CFR 312.40, requirements for administration of an investigational new drug.
milestones.threshold_quote: An investigator may not administer an investigational new drug to human subjects until the IND goes into effect

milestones.title: A human optic-nerve treatment cohort passes an independent safety review permitting dose escalation.
milestones.criterion: The study’s safety monitoring board permits escalation after reviewing an initial treated cohort. On 8 October 2026, Life Biosciences reported that 3 participants with open-angle glaucoma tolerated ER-100 through day 56 without reported dose-limiting toxicities, adverse events of special interest or serious adverse events. The board recommended escalation from 2 × 10^11 to 6 × 10^11 vector genomes. This not-peer-reviewed result concerns early tolerability; regenerated human connections were not demonstrated.
milestones.set_by: Life Biosciences’ ER-100 study safety monitoring board, decision published in the sponsor’s 8 October 2026 announcement; this decision concerns the glaucoma cohort.
milestones.threshold_quote: Data Safety Monitoring Board recommendation was to escalate to Dose Level 2

milestones.title: Controlled human studies provide preliminary evidence that an optic-nerve treatment restores visual function.
milestones.criterion: Controlled studies in patients with a specified optic neuropathy provide preliminary evidence suggesting effectiveness for recovery of lost visual function and characterise common short-term risks. This is the evidential stage FDA identifies before phase 3 investigations. The phase definition supplies no universal acuity gain, responder fraction or follow-up duration for optic-nerve regeneration; these require a treatment-specific protocol.
milestones.set_by: FDA, 21 CFR 312.21(b) and (c), controlled phase 2 studies and the evidential prerequisite for phase 3.
milestones.threshold_quote: after preliminary evidence suggesting effectiveness of the drug has been obtained

milestones.title: Pivotal human studies establish visual benefit and the benefit–risk profile of an optic-nerve treatment.
milestones.criterion: Pivotal studies demonstrate a treatment benefit in the intended optic-neuropathy population and provide the additional effectiveness and safety information needed to evaluate the overall benefit–risk relationship and support physician labeling. For this capability, the proposed indication concerns recovery of pattern vision through regeneration. This is the clinical-evidence stage before the marketing-authorisation decision; the cited FDA framework does not prescribe an optic-nerve-specific numerical endpoint.
milestones.set_by: FDA, published purpose of pivotal phase 3 studies and 21 CFR 312.21(c).
milestones.threshold_quote: demonstrate whether or not a product offers a treatment benefit to a specific population.

not_found: No universal acuity gain, responder fraction or durability threshold for successful optic-nerve regeneration was identified.
No controlled human demonstration of restored vision attributable to regenerated optic-nerve connections was identified.
ClinicalTrials.gov did not provide readable protocol or outcome tables for NCT07290244 through the available pages.
The CNTF-chitosan article’s full text could not be opened through its publisher or PMC pages.
No external completion criterion for biological reconstruction of destroyed human visual cortex was identified.
